title: Hackers Are Weaponizing AI's Habit of Making Things Up
hook: AI coding tools sometimes invent software packages that don't exist. Hackers found they can register those fake names themselves — then wait for AI to recommend their malware to real users.
key_points: Ars Technica reports hackers can use 9 popular AI tools to help assemble massive botnets.
The technique, dubbed 'HalluSquatting,' exploits LLMs hallucinating names of software packages that don't exist.
Attackers register those invented package names themselves, filling them with malicious code.
When an AI tool later 'recommends' that made-up package, unsuspecting users install the attacker's malware instead.
The root cause is familiar: LLMs answer confidently even when they don't actually know — they rarely say 'I don't know.'
content_html: AI coding assistants occasionally hallucinate — they'll confidently suggest installing a software package that doesn't actually exist. Ars Technica reports that hackers have turned that specific weakness into an attack: a technique researchers are calling "HalluSquatting," which they say can be used with 9 of the most popular AI tools to help assemble massive botnets.
extra_html: The mechanics are simple and unsettling. Attackers first figure out (or predict) the kinds of fake package names an AI tool is likely to hallucinate, then register those exact names themselves and fill them with malicious code. When someone later asks an AI coding tool for help and it hallucinates that same invented package as a real recommendation, the user installs the attacker's malware instead of nothing — because the fake package is now sitting there, real and waiting. The root cause is the same one behind every other hallucination story: LLMs are built to keep answering fluently, and they rarely say "I don't know" even when they should. Here, that habit doesn't just produce a wrong sentence — it opens a door for real malware, which is exactly why the same caution that applies to vibe-coded apps applies here: verify what an AI tool tells you to install, especially names you've never seen before.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: The Hidden Risk of Vibe-Coded Apps
related.hook: Anyone can now describe an app and have AI build it — but the AI can quietly leave the doors unlocked. One builder ran his live site for months before noticing a gaping security hole.

related.title: How to Fact-Check AI
related.hook: You can't tell a true AI answer from a made-up one by reading it — both sound equally sure. So build a habit: for anything that matters, verify it somewhere that isn't the AI.

flashcards.explanation_html: It exploits a specific AI weakness — invented package names — by claiming those exact fake names before a user's AI tool recommends installing them.

flashcards.prompt: Why does this attack work in the first place?
flashcards.back_html: LLMs tend to answer confidently even when they don't actually know something, rather than admitting uncertainty — so a made-up package name sounds just as real.

flashcards.prompt: Who is most at risk from HalluSquatting?
flashcards.back_html: Anyone using an AI coding assistant to suggest or install software packages — including non-programmers 'vibe coding' an app who can't easily spot a fake name.
